questions.problem:
$\,$ $x$  is even and $y$ is prime.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$  is even and $y$ is prime" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is even and }y\text{ is prime}) & ≡¬(x\text{ is even}∧y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is even})∨¬(y\text{ is prime}) \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd}∨y\text{ is not prime} \\  & ≡x\text{ is odd or }y\text{ is not prime}.\end{aligned}
$$

De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a<8$ and $a>2$ " is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a<8\text{ and }a>2) & ≡¬(a<8∧a>2) \\  & ≡¬(a<8)∨¬(a>2) \\  & ≡a\ge 8∨a\le 2 \\  & ≡a\ge 8\text{ or }a\le 2.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$a$ is odd and $b$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(a\text{ is odd and }b\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd}∧b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(a\text{ is odd})∨¬(b\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡a\text{ is even}∨b\text{ is even} \\  & ≡a\text{ is even or }b\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}\text{ and }y>\frac{1}{2}) & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3}∧y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le \frac{1}{3})∨¬(y>\frac{1}{2}) \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}∨y\le \frac{1}{2} \\  & ≡x>\frac{1}{3}\text{ or }y\le \frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$\,$ $x\le 0\text{ and }y$ is odd.

The negation of the composite predicate above is the following:

$\,$ 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}{{field-3}}
questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∧B)=¬A∨¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x\le 0\text{ and }y$ is odd" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\le 0\text{ and }y\text{ is odd}) & ≡¬(x\le 0∧y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡¬(x\le 0)∨¬(y\text{ is odd}) \\  & ≡x>0∨y\text{ is even} \\  & ≡x>0\text{ or }y\text{ is even}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$n<0\text{ or }m>-5$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n<0\text{ or }m>-5) & ≡¬(n<0∨m>-5) \\  & ≡¬(n<0)∧¬(m>-5) \\  & ≡n\ge 0∧m\le -5 \\  & ≡n\ge 0\text{ and }m\le -5.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
¬(A∨B)=¬A∧¬B.
$$

So, the negation of "$n$ is positive or $m$ is negative" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n\text{ is positive or }m\text{ is negative }) & ≡¬(n\text{ is positive}∨m\text{ is negative }) \\  & ≡¬(n\text{ is positive})∧¬(m\text{ is negative }) \\  & ≡n\text{ is not positive}∧m\text{ is not negative} \\  & ≡n\text{ is not positive and }m\text{ is not negative}.\end{aligned}
$$

Express the compound predicate above in symbolic form given the following predicates:

- $Q(x):$ $x$ is rational
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The sentence

$\qquad$ $x$ is irrational

can be expressed in symbolic form as $\lnot Q.$

Therefore, the given sentence is expressed symbolically as 

$$
P\lor \lnot Q.
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Negating a Conjunction Using De Morgan's Law
canonical_examples.problem:
$\qquad$ $x$ is prime and $y$ divides $12$.

What is the negation of the composite predicate above?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for conjunctions states that

$$
\neg ( A \land B) = \neg A \lor \neg B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$ is prime and $y$ divides $12$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is prime and }y\text{ divides }12) & ≡¬(x\text{ is prime}∧y\text{ divides }12) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is prime})∨¬(y\text{ divides }12) \\  & ≡x\text{ is not prime}∨y\text{ does not divide }12 \\  & ≡x\text{ is not prime}\text{ or }y\text{ does not divide }12.\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Negating a Disjunction Using De Morgan's Law
canonical_examples.problem:
$\qquad$ $x$ is a multiple of $5$ or $y$ divides $24$.

What is the negation of the composite predicate above?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
De Morgan's law for disjunctions states that

$$
\neg ( A \lor B) = \neg A \land \neg B.
$$

So, the negation of "$x$ is a multiple of $5$ or $y$ divides $24$" is

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(x\text{ is a multiple of [math]5[/math] or }y\text{ divides }24) & ≡¬(x\text{ is a multiple of }5∨y\text{ divides }24) \\  & ≡¬(x\text{ is a multiple of }5)∧¬(y\text{ divides }24) \\  & ≡x\text{ is not a multiple of }5∧y\text{ does not divide }24 \\  & ≡x\text{ is not a multiple of }5\text{ and }y\text{ does not divide }24.\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Logical operations with predicates generalize the corresponding operations on statements. As a result, all the properties of these operations are held.

In particular, for predicates $P(x_1,x_2\ldots,x_n)$ and $Q(y_1,y_2\ldots,y_m),$ De Morgan's laws state the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(P∧Q) & ≡¬P∨¬Q \\ ¬(P∨Q) & ≡¬P∧¬Q\end{aligned}
$$

These can be used to negate open sentences containing conjunctions and disjunctions. For example, let's negate the following:

$$
n \ge 0 \:\textbf{ or }\: 2 \mid m
$$

Applying De Morgan's law for disjunctions, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}¬(n\ge 0\,\text{ or }\,2∣m) & ≡¬(n\ge 0∨2∣m) \\  & ≡¬(n\ge 0)∧¬(2∣m) \\  & ≡n<0∧2∤m \\  & ≡n<0\,\text{ and }\,2∤m.\end{aligned}
$$
